title: Vakkali and the three bodies
hookLine: the Buddha as the truth body, the bliss body and the body that appears in the world
carry: three bodies: truth, glory, and a life on real roads

lines: WHO SEES THE TEACHING SEES ME.
cards: A monk named Vakkali is sick in bed, with one wish: to see the Buddha with his own eyes one more time. Word is sent, and the Buddha comes and sits by him. Vakkali tries to get up; the Buddha tells him to lie still.
Then, instead of a soft word, a sharp question: why do you want to see this foul body? Whoever sees the teaching, he says, sees me. Whoever sees me sees the teaching.
That line is in the Pali texts, and later Buddhists built a whole picture of the Buddha around it.

teach.b: In the Mahayana, the question of what a Buddha is grows into a three-part answer: trikaya, three bodies. Body here means something closer to a form, a way of being present.
First, the truth body, the dharmakaya: the Buddha as truth itself, what was seen on the night of awakening. No edges, no birthday, no address.
When the Buddha told Vakkali that whoever sees the teaching sees him, Mahayana readers heard this body.
Second, the bliss body, the sambhogakaya: the Buddha as the Mahayana sutras describe him in glory, radiant, teaching great bodhisattvas in pure lands, beyond ordinary sight.
Some Tibetan and East Asian practices picture the Buddha this way.
Third, the body that appears, the nirmanakaya: the Buddha who is born, walks the roads, eats rice, falls ill and dies, the life this path followed in its stories.

Here the human life is real, and it is also the truth taking a form people could meet and follow. Some teachers use the moon: the moon itself, its light, and its reflection in a bowl of water. One moon, met three ways.
Schools explain the three bodies differently, and the teaching in this form is Mahayana; Theravada Buddhists speak of the Buddha's life and of the teaching he left, without the three-body scheme.
So where is the Buddha now? In the teaching, for anyone who sees it. In forms suited to whoever is looking.
And in a life once lived on real roads.

how: Mahayana teachers in Tibet and East Asia use the three bodies to explain how the Buddha is present: in the teaching, in visions and pure lands, and in the human life told in the Buddha's story.

o: three ways a Buddha is present: truth, glory, a life
three past lives the Buddha remembered at awakening
the three robes a Buddhist monk is allowed to own

p: the body that appears in the world
wanted to see the Buddha one more time

s: the three bodies are three different Buddhas
they are three ways one Buddha is present: as truth, in glory, and as a human life.
the line about seeing the teaching comes from the Pali texts
the Buddha says it at the bedside of the sick monk Vakkali.
every Buddhist school teaches the three bodies
the three-body teaching is Mahayana, and schools explain it differently.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a sick monk who loves you has begged to see you one more time, and you've come to his bedside. what do you say?
o: stay, and let him look as long as he likes
ask why he wants to see this body, and say whoever sees the teaching sees you
games.why: in the Pali text the Buddha turns him from the body to the teaching. Mahayana readers later heard the truth body in that line.

practice: Bring to mind someone who matters to you and isn't in the room, and notice three ways they're present anyway.
What they stand for, the thing they taught you; how they appear in your mind's eye, a laugh, a way of standing in a doorway; and one real moment when you were actually together.
Rest with all three, then let them go and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Trikaya. Three bodies: the Buddha as the truth itself, as the bliss body in glory, and as the body that appears in the world. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: tri, three, and kaya, body: the three ways a Buddha is present.

carryVoice: Your line: three bodies: truth, glory, and a life on real roads. One Buddha, met three ways. See you tomorrow.
